tasks.name: Compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations
Explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces
Given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity
Explain the purpose of mitigation techniques used to secure the enterprise

concepts.name: Threat actor types
concepts.description: Distinguish nation-state, unskilled attacker, hacktivist, insider threat, organized crime, and shadow IT from scenario evidence.

concepts.name: Threat actor attributes
concepts.description: Compare internal/external position, resources/funding, and sophistication/capability.

concepts.name: Threat actor motivations
concepts.description: Recognize data exfiltration, espionage, disruption, blackmail, financial gain, beliefs, ethical motives, revenge, chaos, and war.

concepts.name: Threat vectors and attack surfaces
concepts.description: Distinguish the route used to attack from the collection of reachable attack points.

concepts.name: Delivery channels
concepts.description: Recognize message, image, file, voice, removable-device, software, and network delivery paths.

concepts.name: Vulnerable and unsupported software
concepts.description: Recognize exposed, vulnerable, client-based/agentless, and unsupported software as attack paths.

concepts.name: Network and exposed-service attack surface
concepts.description: Recognize unsecure networks, open service ports, and default credentials.

concepts.name: Supply-chain attack surface
concepts.description: Recognize MSPs, vendors, and suppliers as indirect trusted paths.

concepts.name: Phishing channels
concepts.description: Distinguish phishing, smishing, and vishing.

concepts.name: Information manipulation and pretexting
concepts.description: Distinguish misinformation, disinformation, and fabricated pretexts.

concepts.name: Impersonation and BEC
concepts.description: Recognize impersonation, business email compromise, and brand impersonation.

concepts.name: Watering holes and typosquatting
concepts.description: Distinguish compromised sites frequented by targets from look-alike or misspelled domains.

concepts.name: Vulnerability model
concepts.description: Recognize a weakness that a threat can exploit or trigger.

concepts.name: Memory vulnerabilities
concepts.description: Distinguish memory injection from buffer overflow.

concepts.name: Race conditions and TOC/TOU
concepts.description: Recognize timing-dependent flaws and time-of-check/time-of-use weaknesses.

concepts.name: Malicious update and OS vulnerabilities
concepts.description: Recognize compromised update paths and operating-system weaknesses.

concepts.name: SQL injection and XSS
concepts.description: Distinguish database-query injection from browser-executed cross-site scripting.

concepts.name: Hardware and lifecycle vulnerabilities
concepts.description: Recognize firmware, end-of-life, and legacy-device risks.

concepts.name: Virtualization vulnerabilities
concepts.description: Recognize VM escape and unsafe resource reuse.

concepts.name: Cloud and supply-chain vulnerabilities
concepts.description: Recognize cloud-specific weaknesses and compromised service, hardware, or software providers.

concepts.name: Cryptographic vulnerabilities and misconfiguration
concepts.description: Recognize weak cryptography and insecure configuration as vulnerability classes.

concepts.name: Mobile and zero-day vulnerabilities
concepts.description: Recognize sideloading, jailbreaking/rooting, and zero-day weaknesses.

concepts.name: Malware behaviors
concepts.description: Distinguish ransomware, trojan, worm, spyware, bloatware, virus, keylogger, logic bomb, and rootkit.

concepts.name: Physical attacks
concepts.description: Recognize physical brute force, RFID cloning, and environmental attacks.

concepts.name: Network attacks
concepts.description: Recognize DDoS, reflection/amplification, DNS, wireless, on-path, credential replay, and malicious-code network activity.

concepts.name: Application attacks
concepts.description: Recognize injection, buffer overflow, replay, privilege escalation, forgery, and directory traversal.

concepts.name: Cryptographic attacks
concepts.description: Distinguish downgrade, collision, and birthday attacks.

concepts.name: Password attacks
concepts.description: Distinguish password spraying from brute-force guessing.

concepts.name: Indicators of malicious activity
concepts.description: Analyze lockouts, concurrent sessions, blocked content, impossible travel, resource anomalies, unusual logging, published indicators, and missing logs.

concepts.name: Mitigation selection
concepts.description: Choose a mitigation that directly reduces the relevant attack path, weakness, or impact.

concepts.name: Segmentation and isolation
concepts.description: Use segmentation or isolation to constrain communication, lateral movement, and blast radius.

concepts.name: Access control and least privilege
concepts.description: Use ACLs, permissions, application allow lists, and least privilege to constrain access and execution.

concepts.name: Patching, configuration enforcement, and decommissioning
concepts.description: Correct known flaws, maintain secure baselines, and remove obsolete assets.

concepts.name: Encryption and monitoring
concepts.description: Use encryption for confidentiality and monitoring for detection and investigation.

concepts.name: Host hardening
concepts.description: Reduce attack surface with endpoint protection, host firewalls/HIPS, service reduction, password changes, and software removal.

questions.prompt: A highly funded team maintains stealthy access to a semiconductor company for a year and steals proprietary research. Which threat actor is MOST consistent with the scenario?
questions.explanation: Long-term stealth, substantial resources, and strategic intellectual-property theft are consistent with nation-state activity, although attribution in real incidents requires evidence.
hints: Look for resources, patience, target value, and strategic goals.

choice_feedback.a: Correct. Long-term access, high resources, and strategic theft are strong nation-state clues.
choice_feedback.b: Organized crime can be highly capable, but financial gain or criminal leverage is usually the stronger clue.
choice_feedback.c: Hacktivists are primarily associated with a cause or ideology.
choice_feedback.d: An insider already has trusted internal access; that is not the key evidence here.

questions.prompt: Why does an internet-facing operating system that is no longer supported by its vendor increase risk?
questions.explanation: Unsupported software increases risk because the vendor may stop supplying security fixes. End-of-life does not automatically make a system unreachable or vulnerable to every attack.
hints: Think about vendor patch support.
